steps.heading: One call, one chart
steps.body: Every Series and DataFrame carries .plot(). It hands the data to matplotlib for you, so you almost never import matplotlib yourself. By default it draws a line and plots against the index — so whatever sits in the index becomes your x-axis.

steps.heading: The default is a line
steps.caption: Dates in the index, revenue on the y-axis. Setting the index is what makes the x-axis a timeline instead of 0, 1, 2…

steps.heading: kind= picks the form
steps.body: Pass kind='bar', 'barh', 'hist', 'scatter' — or use the accessor spelling .plot.bar(), which is the same call. Let the data's job pick the form: bar for comparing categories, line for change over time, hist for the shape of a distribution, scatter for two numeric columns against each other.

steps.heading: Aggregate first, then plot
steps.caption: A groupby result is already one value per category — exactly the shape a bar chart wants. This is the most common plotting line you will write.

steps.heading: Sort before you rank
steps.body: groupby returns groups in key order, not value order, so a bar chart of it comes out alphabetical. If the point is a ranking, sort_values() before plotting — otherwise the reader has to do the comparing you were supposed to do for them.

steps.heading: Same data, readable order
steps.caption: title= and ylabel= are passed straight through to matplotlib. pandas labels the x-axis from the index name for free, but leaves the y-axis to you.

steps.heading: One column per series
steps.body: Plot a whole DataFrame and every column becomes its own series. That is powerful and easy to misuse: two columns on very different scales — revenue near 200, units near 20 — share one y-axis, and the smaller one flattens to nothing. When the scales don't match, draw two charts. The cards ahead drill all of this against the sample table.
